en: Rudrabhaṭṭa:
The First Chapter of the Śṛṅgāratilaka.
He is impassioned (śṛṅgārī) at the face of Girijā, compassionate (sakaruṇa) toward Rati, heroic (pravīra) in [the conquest of] Smara,

loathsome (bībhatso) with his bones, and terrifying (bhayakṛt) with his upraised hood; he is marvelous (adbhuta) by virtue of his lofty form, wrathful (raudra) in the crushing of Dakṣa, laughing (hasakṛt), naked, and finally, serene (praśānta).
Thus may Paśupati, the locus of all aesthetic flavors, lead the virtuous to prosperity.
Possessing a skillful composition of verbs and nouns, with well-jointed transitions, adorned with the qualities and ornaments of excellent speech, full of flavor and composed in beautiful meters—
[this work belongs to] those preeminent poets who have even attained heaven.
Thus, here remains his body composed of poetry, unimpaired.
Although indeed no benefit whatsoever accrues from this work to the wicked, even though it has been composed as a beautiful poem,
nevertheless, for the sake of virtuous people, why should there not be compassion toward this?
Out of fear of lice, there might be the undoing of one's lower garment. // ST_1.3 //
Those whose minds were not pierced by the arrow-like side-glances of joyful women;
who, distressed by the fall into the ocean of saṃsāra, have acted as a boat for others;
and who have condensed the play of boundless Sarasvatī into just two or three words—[to them I bow].
Even above those, the insights of some meritorious soul flash forth.
The establishment of rasa with respect to drama has been explained by Bharata and others;
now, according to my own understanding, this same principle is being declared by me with respect to poetry.
Like a night bereft of the moon, like a woman without her lover,
or like the goddess Lakṣmī without renunciation, our speech does not shine, being devoid of flavor.

It is true that in every house there are good poets, whose eloquence finds honor within their own homes through the virtues born of them, like a noble maiden in her father's mansion; yet such a master of scholars is rare to find, who can grasp the very essence of the speech of those who possess the finest words.
Like a virtuous woman, she is skilled in the full range of arts and capable of stealing the hearts [of all].
Therefore, a poem should be composed with effort so that it is permeated with aesthetic flavor (rasa);
otherwise, for one learned in the sciences, it would cause distress in the assembly.
The erotic, the comic, the pathetic, the furious, the heroic, the terrible,
the loathsome, the marvelous, and the tranquil— these nine are remembered as the aesthetic flavors (rasas) in poetry.
Love, mirth, sorrow, anger, energy, fear, as well as disgust, wonder, and tranquility are proclaimed to be the stable emotions (sthāyibhāvas). ST 1.10.
Disgust, as well as exhaustion, apprehension, envy, pride, fatigue, indolence, dejection, anxiety, delusion, fortitude, and memory. (1.11)
Shame, fickleness, joy, agitation, as well as dullness, pride, despondency, longing, sleep, and epilepsy; ST 1.12.
Sleep, awakening, indignation, as well as dissimulation, ferocity, mental confusion, disease, madness, and even death.
Terror and apprehension are to be known as transitory states;
these thirty-three emotions attain the status of aesthetic flavors (rasas).
Stupefaction, perspiration, horripilation, breaking of the voice, trembling, change of color, tears, and fainting—these eight are known as the *sāttvika* [emotions]. (ST 1.15)
These very entities, when perfectly developed, attain the state of being tastes, just as distinct substances [attain the state of] having the nature of sweet and other tastes. (ST 1.16)
Just as flowers, leaves, fruits, and so forth arise upon a tree,
in the same way, delightful particularities in the form of entities arise within the aesthetic flavor (*rasa*).
Generally, no poetic work is found here that possesses only a single flavor; rather, whichever flavor predominates is designated by its corresponding name. (ST 1.18)
Kaiśikī, Ārabhaṭī, Sātvatī, and likewise Bhāratī—
these four modes (vṛttis) are to be known as indicators of the manifestation of aesthetic flavors (rasa).
From dharma comes wealth, from wealth comes desire, and from desire arises the fruit of happiness;
for the successful attainment of these, the erotic sentiment (śṛṅgāra) with its hero as the protagonist is most effective.
The physical gestures of men and women that arise from passion,
whether in union or in separation, are considered the two-fold erotic sentiment (śṛṅgāra).
Furthermore, this [love] is of two kinds: union between those who are joined and separation between those who are parted;
and again, it is twofold as being either concealed or manifest. (ST 1.22)
Her beloved placed his fingers all around her pair of breasts, which resembled the frontal globes of the elephant of passion, even though they bore the marks of his fingernails on the left side.
She considered her right hand to be her beloved.
Distressed by sighs that repeatedly break forth from his throat and swirl around him like the fifth note, and drenched on all sides by falling tears, he—
distraught by separation from his beloved— has abandoned the redness of her lower lip.
Now I think he practices a vow as difficult as turbulent fire and water.

When her lover, whose passion was kindled by the various sequences of amorous play, arrived at the rendezvous, that fawn-eyed woman uttered some indistinct cooing, by which her bed— [Note: The provided text fragment ends abruptly. The translation reflects the partial nature of the source.]
Not surrounded by the lowly throngs of noisy chatterers,
her glance— curved slightly as her throat-stalk turned toward the petals of her full breasts, and causing her thin bodice to ripple— was then cast by that deer-eyed woman.
And those words, clever with their artful sentiments, expand the workings of love;
alas, O mind, do you remember them? Desired actions are accomplished through merits.
Generous, of noble birth, skilled in amorous pleasures, capable, proficient in the arts, youthful,
wealthy, auspicious, patient, fortunate, and proud.
In this world, however, the hero should be one who is desired by women. // ST_1.23 //
In this regard, there are four types—namely the compliant, the clever, the deceitful, and the impudent;
their charming illustrations will now be stated by way of their actions. (ST 1.24)
Because of his intense passion for her, he always abandoned other women;
thus, he is remembered as being "favorable" (anukūla), just like Rāma was toward Sītā.
"Friend, our garments are not beautiful, our necklace is not radiant,
our gait is not haughty, nor is our laughter loud, and we have no pride at all;
yet even other people say that her beloved is charming only because of her."
We consider the entire world to be suffering by this much alone: that it casts its gaze [upon such things]. (ST 1.25a)
He who does not abandon respect, fear, love, and sincere affection for his former wife, even when his mind is directed elsewhere, should be known as one who is "right-handed" (dakṣiṇa).
That very same prostration, that very same speech, those same playful gestures, that same fear, and that same sweetness of jesting appropriate for former affection—
yet you, acting as an unkind wife toward your beloved, speak of them as being defiled by faults.
"O friend, why does my mind thus waver day and night with anxiety? (ST 1.26a)
He speaks pleasant words in one’s presence but elsewhere acts most harshly;
having committed an offense, he conceals his conduct—such a person is crooked and deceitful.
"We two are naturally fickle, yet we are both possessed of great learning;

however, you two here are truly disciplined. Therefore, regarding this offender who is nonetheless our lover, tell us: is it proper for us to enjoy ourselves with him again, or not? Alas, such was our conversation!
When her ears had certainly reached [the eyes], the fawn-eyed woman turned her eyes toward them to inquire.
Moreover,
out of anger, having violently seized him by the hair even as he was bowing slightly, the beloved led him forcefully many times with her necklace into the chamber of passion.
"Will you go back to her house?"— thus a certain fortunate man is secretly struck by the ear-lotus of a woman who repeatedly utters words with syllables choked in her throat;
he is now free from fear, though he has committed an offense, and he is neither embarrassed nor reproached.
He is described as being impudent, even though he has incurred the fault of false speech and wrong view.
While I was speaking harshly in anger, he forcibly kissed my face; though his hand was repeatedly struck by mine, he quickly seized it with his own, and then,
before my friends, he placed the blows of his feet upon my head.
"I do not know, friend, how I can now be angry with that lover.
Furthermore:
"Fie on you, shameless rogue! Let that very same beloved woman be courted by you."
"Since this lac-dye explains upon your heart the blow from the sole of her foot"—
even when addressed thus, if this wicked person, skilled in false speech, does not indeed release my feet, then what else can I do, O friend? (ST 1.28b)
He should be one who keeps counsel secret, pure, eloquent, devoted, and skilled in jesting;
he should serve as his companion in pleasure, capable of appeasing even an angry woman.
The *pīṭhamarda*, the *viṭa*, and the *vidūṣaka*—thus he is threefold. Among these, the first is one who follows the heroine and the hero. (ST 1.30)

The *viṭa* is said to possess a single branch of knowledge, while the *vidūṣaka* is primarily devoted to playfulness; he creates laughter through his own physical appearance, dress, and speech, and is an expert in jesting.
The conventional usage regarding the continuity of these [moments] is generally abundant;
nevertheless, although each has been illustrated, some further examples are now being stated.
Relinquish this pride and make the words of your virtuous friends bear fruit;
why do you with vain distress emaciate your body, which is born of passion? Now, honor your beloved who bows at the edge of your feet with all his heart.
O deluded one, once time—the deer—has departed, it does not have the power to return.
O high-minded lady, do not maintain excessive pride toward that lover;
for what else remains for you apart from this [man], whether he be right or wrong? Even he, at this very moment, may become like the fire of universal destruction.
The moon possesses a luster like the sliced surface of a lotus root.

By your sighs— sprouting from afar, spreading through your heart, tumbling in your throat, forced out through your mouth, and escaping with great heat as they struggle through your constricted nostrils— the intense fever born of mighty love has been clearly revealed.
What is the use of this graceful arching of the eyebrows toward her beloved? Why this anger?
His heroines here are threefold: his own wife, the wife of another, and the common woman, all of whom are skilled in the full range of the arts. (ST 1.33)

Devoted to the conduct of the city (paurācāra), virtuous, and adorned with forgiveness and straightforwardness—the innocent (mugdhā), the intermediate (madhyā), and the bold (pragalbhā)—are considered the three types of one's own wife (svakīyā). ST 1.34.
There, the charming young bride, adorned with fresh youth,
though ignorant of the secrets of the new god of love, experienced a pleasure that was almost entirely overcome by bashfulness.
Her pair of eyes reaches as far as the vicinity of her ears and yet they long to spread further;
her breasts have begun to resemble jars and yet they desire to support her chin;
and though the expanse of her hips is already heavy, it still seeks greater weight.
I believe that the deer-eyed maiden finds no satisfaction whatsoever in her youth.
Since there is this horripilation upon the surface of her breasts with glistening beads of perspiration, and since her gaze falls askance and suddenly contracts,
I suspect that the lover has tasted a portion of her passion.
The mind is neither neutral, nor is it upright and pleasant, nor is it firm.
"Stop, O Lord! Release the hem of my garment;
extinguish this lamp; this is our vow, my friend!"—by these words of the newlywed bride, the young man [was moved].
She attained even greater joy than from sweet words;
when embraced, she turns her face away with a tremble during a kiss, yet after turning back, she remains for a long time upon the bed and desires to dally. (ST_1.35c–1.36)
When she steals his mouth during a kiss,
turns away when being embraced on the bed, and trembles excessively; and when spoken to, she says something indistinct even though addressed repeatedly— [these are the signs].
A newlywed wife delights his heart exceedingly within.
He wins over the innocent girl by conciliating her with gentle means,
rather than through terrifying dispositions or childish threats that cause excessive fear.
"O fair-faced one, I think this swarm of wandering bees is fleeing from the edge of the lake toward the lotus, turning its back because of its thirst for your mouth,"—
when this was said, she turned her neck slightly in fear.
The young woman was kissed for a long time on her lotus-like face by her husband.
Even when he is pursuing another woman, if that beloved becomes angry, she weeps before him; and when conciliated even slightly, she is satisfied.
When pride was first aroused, that young bride, not recognizing any other change in him, wept bitterly;
then the rogue, having thoroughly wiped away the water from her eyes, [embraced her firmly].
And having kissed her lower lip, she was brought to a state of grace.
The *madhyā* heroine has ascended to the prime of youth; the god of love has manifested within her; her speech is somewhat bold, and she possesses a degree of variety in amorous dalliance. (ST 1.39)
The tremulous eye exhausts even the vision of sages;
whose heart does not become heartless when overcome by a pair of breasts?
Her gait has slowed, stealing away the movement of those possessed by the god of love.
In her youth, everything belonging to the slender maiden triumphs equally.
Her gaze clings deeply to her beloved; her speech, full of wit, is devoted to him;
her hand has abandoned all other tasks to arrange the garland of her locks;
her chest is covered again and again; and she moves with a languor born of the weight of her emotion.
"O fair-browed one, why has this delightful state of yours arisen so suddenly?
O fortunate one, are you the *kuravaka* tree to us, or is it the *kesara* tree dwelling in our hearts, longing for the wine of your face with its embrace?"
"A kick is surely appropriate for you,
O Aśoka," said a certain woman charmingly in jest, as if it were a favor.
In that manner, the fawn-eyed woman, her passion aroused during amorous dalliances, somehow managed to manifest such cleverness toward her lover,
as was repeatedly echoed by the cooing of the birds.
It was as if hundreds of domestic pigeons had become her disciples.
She intensely engages with her beloved as if in love-play;
she seems to enter into his limbs and appears to faint in pleasure.

Having performed various kinds of amorous play with passion, she finally attained rest after a long time; her pair of eyes were closed in bliss and the surface of her cheeks was moist with perspiration.
Thinking, "This beautiful woman has indeed fallen asleep," the fortunate man embraced her freely in that very same position.
His body, unable to endure the intense friction of love's limbs, fell asleep along with her.

The *dhīrā* (self-controlled woman) speaks with indirect speech (*vakrokti*) to her beloved who has committed an offense out of anger; the *madhyā* (moderate woman) weeps while offering reproaches; and the *adhīrā* (unsteady woman) speaks harshly. (ST 1.41)
Approaching her, you were eager for a firm embrace;
after a long time, your beautiful sandalwood paste was wiped away, and instantly, by kissing her eyes, you took up the collyrium upon them.
O dear one, you have already realized here and now that your purpose has been fulfilled.
When I am enraged, O Lord, the moon acts as the sun, the lotuses become heaps of glowing coals, and the trunks of your plantain trees turn into firebrands;
indeed, that time was of one nature, but now this other time has become poisonous, though it was once composed of nectar.
"Shame on you, O rogue! The helpless woman, shedding tears and weeping in delusion, has departed."
O rogue, along with hundreds of your desires, that very same beloved— delightful through her artificial emotions— remains fixed in your mind;
for us, there is indeed no room here at all.
Therefore, enough with these mockeries of falling at her feet!
A woman who has secured her future should be bold and skilled in all the arts of love, such that she firmly overcomes the man and shines with radiant charms.
This is that very *paraṅginī* lotus-stalk which my beloved takes and makes into a necklace upon the slope of my breasts, possessing the luster of a fresh star;
and this is that very *bandhūka* flower, O friend, which he has torn apart to part his hair with it.
It will bear the splendor of the arrows of the flower-bowed god who desires to conquer all hopes.
Where the sandalwood paste is sufficiently wiped away by trickling drops of sweat, where the tinkling of anklets is drowned out by unrestrained moans,
and where all objects of the senses quickly attain a state of singular focus upon desire.
O friends, I speak of that sexual union for the sake of delight; as for everything else, it is merely the way of the world.
"O Lord, O playful one, arrange my forehead with its curling locks and its tilaka;
O Master of my life, join back the necklace broken upon the slope of my breast.
Having spoken thus, she whose face was like the full moon felt the bliss of the conclusion of lovemaking.
Touched by him, she said "So be it," her hair standing on end with thrill, yet she fell once more into a state of enchantment—

[charmed] by his sweet words, by the knitting of his brows, by the threatening gestures of his fingers, and by the languid, swaying movements of his limbs which were like the very kinsmen of a great festival.
With her expansive side-glances cast again and again,
she assists the five-arrowed god in his conquest of the three worlds;
untroubled in love, she seems to melt into the limbs of her beloved.
Who is this? From where am I? Or what is this delight that he does not perceive through his own aesthetic essence?
Blessed are those women, O friend, who, even when their beloved has embraced them with all his limbs, summon great fortitude and display boldness in the act of seduction;
for as for us, we must have our garment loosened even by his lotus-like hand.
Who is this? Who am I here? Why indeed does no memory of the sexual union arise? (ST 1.43a)
Even when he has committed a fault, that virtuous woman does not take offense at him out of anger;
rather, concealing her outward expression, she remains indifferent toward him as if she were engaged in lovemaking.

I perceive that speech which is so clever in its abundant courtesy, that respectful rising from afar, and this seat offered with her own hand— even though it has been broken; and I perceive how she repeatedly casts her gaze right toward her friend.
I suspect, O lotus-eyed one, that some powerful displeasure toward me has arisen within you.
That her hand was not warded off while loosening the knot of her garment;
that she did not knit her brows even slightly while her lower lip was repeatedly bitten;

and that her body was offered, as it were, without hesitation for her husband’s embrace—oh! (Note: The phrase *saumudgranthayan* appears to be a typographical error for *samudgranthayan*. The translation reflects the intended meaning.)
By that very man, acting with conciliatory conduct, the great anger of the proud woman was appeased.
The moderate woman pierces him with well-spoken words accompanied by gentle irony;
the impatient woman strikes him down like a lover by means of threats.

Enough with these false lamentations; desist, O lover! It has long been known to you that she alone is your beloved. Go forth boldly to her, for by her nail-marks and her playful gestures, she has already taken firm root in your heart.
What service can I possibly perform for you, who are surely devoted to upright conduct?
"Very well, you shall be watched by me," she said, firmly binding her arms with a garland;
"you shall see her again, you rogue!"— thus repeatedly threatening her beloved, she,
intent on concealment before her friends, moved with jingling anklets out of anger.
By the act of striking with her feet, the beloved was made into an *aśoka* tree by the proud woman.
The *mugdha* and the *punarbhū* are considered to be of one and the same type; therefore, because the distinction between these two is extremely subtle, it has not been demonstrated by the poets.
Furthermore, the *madhyā* (intermediate) and the *pragalbhā* (bold) are each divided into two types,
according to whether they are the senior (*jyeṣṭhā*) or junior (*kaniṣṭhā*) in relation to the hero’s affection.
Due to constraint as well as affection, the hero, though full of passion,
generally acts toward her like one skilled in the arts.
Thinking "these are two blue water-lilies," I closed my eyes with great affection, thinking, "I shall restrain them";
then, her cheeks were intensely thrilled with horripilation.
The youth kissed the woman deeply and secretly.
In prosperity, in adversity, and even at the time of death, love arises for that which is one's own; such is the case for the doer of merit.
O beloved, those belonging to another are said to be of two kinds: the maiden and the married woman; they become objects of desire for you either by sight or by hearing, as the case may be.

In such a manner, the young woman gazed at the face of her beloved with glances that were playful and tender in one way, slightly contracted in another, and curved in yet another, as if they were laughing at the arrows of the God of Love.
Even the assembly of friends, though skilled in graceful arts, was utterly amazed.
Having heard that enchanting voice from outside, another lotus-eyed woman looked out;
yet, after that [voice], there was not even a sesame seed’s worth remaining for her ears to hear.
Seeing him whom she had long heard was "fortunate," that woman’s eyes closed as passion took hold;
and observing her body rendered motionless, the eunuchs [realized].
The women of the inner apartments, their minds distressed, [longed for him] as for a husband.
O mind, why do you desire to see that very beloved who is so difficult to find— even though you have heard enough about him, he causes emaciation, sleeplessness, and distress?
His vision of that [object] occurs in three ways: directly, in a painting, or likewise in a dream;
and his hearing of it occurs in the same manner, according to place, time, and modality.
Truly, in every house there are beloved deer-eyed women, whose bodies become rivers of pure, intoxicating nectar surging from the activity of their lovers’ embraces;
yet here is another, some other fortunate man, at the mere sight of whom the body [is transformed].
Through perspiration, yawning, trembling, fear, and other such signs, one attains a certain state visible to the eyes.

O friend, although he is depicted in a painting, this man, who resembles the God of Love, forcibly uproots my shame and agitates my heart with longing. A simple girl, upon the arrival of her beloved in a dream, [is thrilled] by the touch of his hand.

Having signaled her anger with her creeper-like body covered in horripilation, she suddenly cried out repeatedly, "Do not touch me! Do not touch me! Though empty of meaning, she was not laughed at by her friend; on the contrary, she was repeatedly grieved for with concern.

O dear friend, this mansion with its brilliantly shimmering lamps, this honey with its blue lotuses, and this sweet singing— all of this will indeed be fruitful for you, provided that he should be here.
O slender-limbed one, the cluster of night-lotuses blooms, the breeze from the lake blows, and the moon kisses the sky;
how can your delight be without him? (ST 1.51e)
Let there be the non-arising of your eyes, and let there be the complete non-existence of your breasts,
if that youth is not seen, nor is he embraced with fervor.
It is clear that this maiden is unable to look at or speak to him openly,
even in private, because of her modesty when he gazes at her and addresses her.
Though she does not look at her beloved, she gazes at him intensely;
though she does not speak even when addressed, she speaks with great care— thus,
due to the interplay of shame and love, she behaves toward her lord of the heart.
The fool bears this charming variety of flavors.
A female friend whose mind has perceived the heroine speaks to the hero, or the hero speaks to her friend, in order to manifest her love, as follows: (ST 1.53)
With her body’s hair standing on end and her eyes closing like buds out of modesty,
this young woman, O moon among men, longs for the touch of your hand, just as the night-lily longs for the moonlight.
That these rays of the cool-rayed moon cause such torment,
that these breezes from the blossoming lotuses cause such delusion,
and that this body suffers exhaustion— this is the fault.
O fair-limbed one, it belongs to your friend alone, who is possessed of abundant modesty.
Not seeing her beloved, she gazes with wide-open eyes;
from afar, she looks intently at her friend as if she were her own kin.
Smiling without apparent cause, she says something to her friend,
and with some pretext, she reveals a certain beautiful limb.
She arranges again her garland and girdle which had been set aside by her friend,
and performs charming gestures with the graceful movements of her limbs.
When her beloved approached her, though she spoke to him many times,
the deer-eyed woman remained silent with her face cast down; then, indeed, he was gazed upon by her in that manner, with a playful and sidelong look.
I think that somehow, as she was seen, she must have transgressed the bounds of propriety;

for her slender body was bent sideways, her unevenly turned breasts struck against one another so that the pearl necklace snapped, and her cheeks were bristling with horripilation and glistening with perspiration.
When he signaled for her to look from afar, she, whose passion was irresistible, cast her gaze upon his face and embraced her companion tightly.
That she laughs without cause and speaks to her friend without reason— this is the sign of love.
Beholding her beloved, she declares herself to be dependent upon him.
Raising her vine-like arm, which was graceful with the luster of its root— the emerging wound—
she appeared beautiful with a pearl necklace swaying against the surface of her heaving, full breasts;
she summoned the God of Love by the sound of the bracelets on her trembling fingertips.
The scratching of her ear by that slender maiden, whose eyes are curved, is triumphant.
Having caught sight of her beloved for a moment, she fastens her ear-ornament and girdle upon him;
yet, she gives them back to her friends once again.
Each limb was like a dwelling place for the god of love.
As if for the pleasure of her lover, the mass of rays from her teeth was raised by a yawn, appearing like a string of hanging pearls,
while the elaborate display of her vine-like arms met above her head.

Another [woman], having cast aside [her husband] through pride, enters his heart like a seven-arched gateway; yet another, though married to someone else, acts entirely like one whose passion is unrestrained,
just as a woman in a wretched state approaches her lover of her own accord.
Having indeed transgressed my friend’s words, cast aside all appropriate modesty,
abandoned the weight of fear, and set aside even a trace of pride in my own good fortune,
I have surely taken only the command of the preceptor Manmatha.
O crest-jewel among the entire host of the elegant, you have taken refuge [in him].
Her eyes close with joy, her hips even exude moisture,
and her slender body trembles at the sight of him, just as it did before.
At the place of rendezvous, the young woman— her eyes languid with passion, her hands busy grasping her slipping girdle,
her face drenched by the sweat flowing from the heavy burden of love, and her limbs paralyzed by trembling—
even as he cooed endearingly to every part of her body, remained full of curiosity.
"Let him stay; alas, even to look upon my beloved has not been granted."
Though she is ill at ease due to her bashfulness, she does not herself approach him out of modesty;
however, her friend should describe her condition to her beloved as follows.
O fortunate one, during her separation from you, her sighs faltered over the seeds of the plantain tree,
and the space between her breasts was drenched by the tears falling with a *chham* sound; thus,
O handsome one, did her emaciation come to pass.
By which the ring suddenly slips from its place upon the finger. (ST_1.60a)
A woman who has no other refuge, who belongs to herself, and who cannot be taken by wealth—she is the "wife of another" (parāṅganā) [in this context];
for her love alone [is the criterion], and thus she is considered [as such] by those who possess passion.
A courtesan is a woman common to all; she desires only wealth.
She feels neither aversion toward one devoid of merit nor attachment toward one possessed of virtue.
The true nature of these [women] has been declared by some; we, however, shall speak again, describing their state of passion through this very reasoning.

In these women, there is only a semblance of the erotic sentiment (śṛṅgārābhāsa) and never the erotic sentiment itself; or else, has their passion been devoured by cranes? Or perhaps it is their very activity [that is so]. (ST 1.64)
Therefore, might they too possess passion for someone? Or rather, is it altogether absent? For the sake of wealth, they delude the vulgar with artificial emotions.

One who bears the marks of a religious order, one whose desires are concealed, one who considers himself a man despite being impotent, one who has acquired wealth easily, a fool, and one who is arrogant because of his father’s fortune. ST 1.66.
Having first recognized such men as commoners and having seized their wealth, these women treat them like strangers and torment them. (ST 1.67)
But for them, who are skilled in the arts of love-play, there arises a delightful sexual union that causes all other women to be forgotten. (ST 1.68)
Marked by the pressing of breast-slopes in a firm embrace, by perspiring cheeks,
by bitten lips and uttered sighs, by wildly wandering brows and dancing hands,
The fortunate man attains dalliance with courtesans, who are the abode of fortitude for the flower-bowed god of love.
There is no jealousy toward wives of noble family,
nor is there unrestrained dalliance with the wives of others; yet both of these traits are fully developed in courtesans.
Oh, all this is the very property of Love!
Having been reduced to ashes long ago by the flames of the fire from the eye of the wrathful wielder of the Pināka bow,
I believe that Kāma is brought back to life once more by the glances of courtesans.
When served with skill, they bring delight; otherwise, they destroy.
By their very nature, they are difficult to understand; therefore, courtesans are like poison.
The woman whose husband is under her own control, the one longing for him, likewise the one adorned for the tryst,
the one who has been deceived by his failure to meet, the one who has been slighted, and the woman going to meet her lover.
And the heroine whose beloved is away has likewise been previously indicated; these same heroines here become eightfold again according to their various conditions.
She whose husband, drawn by the qualities of her passion, does not leave her side,
is like a woman who has her husband under her own control and is devoted to various amorous dalliances.
He draws a leaf-design upon her breasts, fastens a garland around her neck,
applies a forehead-mark while smoothing her hair from her cheeks, and thus,

In this manner, this erotic sentiment (śṛṅgāra) should always be fashioned by poets;
for a poem devoid of it is generally said to be flavorless.
Having reflected thus, the connoisseur of aesthetic flavor (rasajña), employing abundant practice, composes this [work] as flavor;
that poem, having been placed upon the station of the learned, [attains its goal].
The universe wanders about within the mouths.
Thus ends the second chapter, named "Separation," in the *Śṛṅgāratilaka*, a treatise on poetic sentiments and figures of speech composed by Śrī Rudrabhaṭṭa.
The Third Chapter.
The comic sentiment (hāsya) arises from distorted limbs, speech, actions, and dress;
because it is rooted in laughter, it occurs across three types of characters, as follows. (ST 3.1)

and teeth just barely visible— this is how it should be for those who are supreme.
A bracelet on his hand, the lord of serpents with upraised hood, eyes like blazing fire, a throat curved by the neutralized Kālakūṭa poison, and a garment of the skin of a great elephant—
this is the beautiful attire of the bridegroom to captivate the eye of Gaurī; such is my thought.
May the emergence of laughter from Paśupati, manifested by the swelling of his cheeks, protect you!
This [laughter] becomes for those of middle standing one with an open-lotus face;
for the lowly, it is like falling tears accompanied by audible sound.
"O innocent one, O fortunate lady, you do not yet understand the workings of love; surely this bee, seeking lotuses, has mistaken your husband’s lip for one.
Thus did her friend laugh at the bride with such manifest joy.
Just as bees, delighting in the fragrance of the liquor within the mouth, have rushed forward.

"Alas, what a pity! These hunters, having seen your extraordinary state in the abode of your enemies, have discarded *guñjā* berries and placed pearl ornaments upon the breasts of the women; they have put lotuses in their ears instead of peacock feathers.

With eyes moistened by tears, they laugh aloud together with their wives.

In this state, falling to the ground, reviling fate, weeping, wretched cries, beating one's body, delusion, and discoloration of the complexion arise. (ST 3.6)

With the weight of blood flowing out from the ends of my channels, I shall satisfy the wrath [of the gods].

In this [state], there occurs the reddening of the face, the brandishing of weapons, perspiration, trembling, the seizing of the lower lip, the display of power, the striking with the hand, and the knitting of the brows. (ST 3.8)

Capable of uplifting all sentient beings without exception.

In that state, there arise fortitude, pride, agitation, intelligence, mindfulness, and horripilation;
as well as various interruptions of speech, along with enthusiasm and the force of indignation.

This state of being a locus of fear, arising from distorted sounds and other such stimuli, becomes the aesthetic flavor (rasa) known as the Terrible (bhayānaka); its suggested relishers (vodṛ) are children, women, and low-born characters.
Hearing the sound of trumpets at the gate, the innocent child of the fortunate man— his creeper-like arms trembling with fear and grey with dust— clings to his father’s neck.
Driven away by a woman full of indignation due to the occurrence of a lovers' quarrel— even though he had bowed at her lotus feet and displayed millions of endearments—
she was [later] drawn back by another woman who was terrified by the roar of a fresh rain-cloud.
The lord of her life embraced her, whose delicate necklace was broken.
O Lord of the Earth, with all their limbs paralyzed by trembling and with drops of perspiration trickling down, they began to address you.
The enemies acted like women.
Change of complexion, tears, terror, trembling of the hands, feet, and so forth, perspiration, dryness of the mouth, looking about, and agitation are proclaimed [as the signs]. (ST 3.13)

The *bībhatsa* (the loathsome) is to be known as having the nature of disgust (*jugupsā*), arising from the sight, hearing, or even the mention of unpleasant objects such as putrid matter and the like. (ST 3.14)
It is filled with the rotting corpses of writhing worms, steeped in the stench of flowing blood and fat, pervaded by the foul odor emanating from a succession of decaying carcasses,
teeming with swarming birds, and where the dance of death unfolds within its three junctions.
The cemetery, filled with demons skilled in their arts, shone forth.
Covering the nose, contracting the face, hiding the body, spitting, and so forth may occur even toward superior beings due to agitation. (ST 3.15)
The aesthetic flavor (rasa) consisting of wonder is to be known by those expert in flavors as arising from magic, sorcery, celestial women, groves, and the like. (ST 3.16)
"O swan, it is true that you have carried off this woman; such is the fate of women.
Nevertheless, these others wander about—this is a wondrous feat of illusion."
In this state, there arise stammering, cries of "well done," perspiration, horripilation, trembling, steadiness of the gaze, and its expansion. (ST 3.17)
Arising from perfect knowledge, he is peaceful through equanimity toward all living beings; having extinguished both darkness and passion, he is the Leader who has transcended desire for that state.
Day after day, wealth was given to supplicants according to their desires;
the host of enemies was reduced to nothing but women by the prowess of his own sword;
and for a long time, love was bestowed upon those dear to him who were overflowing with affection.
What else remains for us to do beyond this? We have no regard even for our own bodies.
For here the mind, being without support, remains firmly established in the Self;
there is no desire for pleasure, nor does agitation arise even toward suffering.
Regarding those eight rasas previously mentioned, it is certain that among them there are two pairs of opposing rasas; one should avoid their combination.
The erotic and the loathsome sentiments, as well as the heroic and the terrifying,
the furious and the marvelous, and likewise the comic and the pathetic, are mutually antagonistic.
From the erotic (*śṛṅgāra*) arises the comic (*hāsya*); from fierce action (*raudrakarman*), the pathetic (*karuṇa*);
likewise, from the heroic (*vīra*), the marvelous (*adbhuta*); and from the loathsome (*bībhatsa*), the terrifying (*bhayānaka*). (ST 3.22)

Regarding these two aesthetic moods (rasa) which have been described by the wise as the "produced" and the "producer," even if their blending is effected through artifice, it is certainly not defective.

Certain transitory states (bhāvas) that were previously shown within the divisions of the aesthetic flavors (rasas) are here proclaimed in their own right; they are considered beautiful by the wise. (ST 3.24)

These states, beginning with love (rati) and so forth, indicate the intention of the aesthetic flavor (rasa); they consist of fifty [types]: the permanent (sthāyin), the transitory (saṃcārin), and the involuntary (sāttvika). Understand them. (ST 3.25)
The mental states (bhāvas), such as love (rati) and the rest, are traditionally held to reside only within the aesthetic sentiments (rasas) like the erotic (śṛṅgāra).
Furthermore, when each of these is considered in terms of its stability, thirty-three other mobile states (carāḥ) are traditionally enumerated.
Generally, when the mind is unsettled, phenomena arise in a state of confusion;
yet they are described here in their true nature as they actually exist.
Doubt, envy, fear, languor, disease, anxiety, memory, fortitude, longing, amazement, joy, shame, madness, and likewise intoxication; ST 3.28.
Despair, dullness, sleep, dissimulation, restlessness, and forgetfulness—
these transitory states (vyabhicāribhāvas) are to be employed in the erotic sentiment (śṛṅgāra).
Fatigue, restlessness, sleep, dreaming, as well as exhaustion, apprehension, envy, and dissimulation— these are the emotional states that arise in the comic (hāsya).

Miserliness, anxiety, as well as exhaustion, despondency, dullness, forgetfulness, and disease— these states are to be known in the context of compassion by those skilled in the nature of mental states.
Joy, envy, as well as pride, enthusiasm, and intoxication,
restlessness, ferocity, and impetuosity— these are proclaimed to be the emotional states (*bhāvas*) in the Furious (*raudra*) sentiment.
Impatience, awakening, deliberation, then intelligence, fortitude,
anger, envy, tears, delusion, agitation, and horripilation.
Pride, intoxication, and ferocity—these states occur in the heroic [rasa];
while terror and death are to be described as occurring in the fearsome [rasa].
Epilepsy, despondency, fear, agitation, mental confusion, intoxication,
and madness— these are to be known as the states arising from the loathsome (bībhatsa).
Agitation, stupefaction, delusion, wonder, exhilaration, and mental reflection—
these are the transitory emotions (bhāvas) that the wise bind to this marvelous rasa.
In this way, the transitory mental states (bhāvas) should be understood as residing within each individual rasa;
however, these sāttvika states exist as the substratum for all rasas.

That [poetry] which possesses dance, song, intoxication, and enjoyment; which has charming compositions consisting of descriptions of dress and limbs; which is endowed with sweetness; and which is beautiful due to its few compounds.
This speech is remembered here as the Kaiśikī style.
This mode (vṛtti) should be employed with effort by the wise for the enhancement of the sentiments of love, humor, and compassion. (ST 3.39)
"The beauty of the moon is falsely extolled by poets; where indeed is the loveliness of the lotus, its radiance shattered by the touch of night?
Having reflected thus for a long time, she gazed at the lovely, shimmering luster of the deer-eyed woman.
With their faces raised by fresh youth, they gaze at one another; I think their breasts are gazing upon their face.
This is the graceful hand of the flower-armed god, the eye of the splendor of passion, the sole abode of good fortune, the touchstone of charm, and the banner of success in wit;
it is the secret witness of some hidden treasury of playfulness, whose kinsman is intoxication.
"Friend, let this fresh nail-mark on your armpit be concealed with a cloth."
Even the brilliant radiance of their shimmering golden earrings became a source of intense distress for those whose lotus-like faces were made beautiful by amorous women.
Within them, fires that were not small blazed up intensely.
It abounds in the confusion of variegated combat and the falling of weapons, enriched by illusions, sorcery, leaps, and bounds,
and is firmly bound with vigorous and weighty syllables.
This mode of expression is to be known by the wise as *sārabhaṭī*.
In the Furious, the Terrible, and the Disgusting sentiments, this style, which creates the beauty of poetry, is thus employed by the discerning.
With pearls drenched in blood dripping from the frontal globes of elephants split open by weapons;
appearing like a vast, flickering mass of light due to its expansive and shimmering radiance;
with the tips of swords gleaming as they are brandished by a steady, furious troop leaping forth; and possessing a fierce, formidable onset.
Then that battle became difficult to withstand, with great warriors seized by the wives of the Siddhas.
"This is not the roar of thunder, but the deep and harsh sound of his trumpets; these are not clouds with the luster of the coils of fearsome serpents, but his dust.
Thus, O Lord, at the time of the new monsoon, [the enemy] was agitated by the suspicion that it was your army.
With the luster of their faces fading, women who oppose them tremble and perish.
Drinking blood, relishing flesh, and dragging along a garland of entrails,
this jackal wanders through this great battle crowded with headless trunks.

That which is characterized by a preponderance of joy and an abundance of virtuous conduct, which is delightful through its noble speech and supreme generosity, and which is blessed with marvelous attainments;
This mode of performance is considered here to be the Sātvatī.

This mode of expression is considered appropriate for the heroic, the furious, the marvelous, and the peaceful sentiments; it possesses a wealth of meaning that is not overly obscure and is delightful with its pleasant-sounding words, as follows: ST 3.43.
"You are the progenitor of Lakṣmī and the treasury of the waters; you alone, O ocean, are the inexhaustible mine of all jewels and remain steadfast within your bounds—who else could speak otherwise?
Yet, for the submarine fire that has entered your single abode, there is constant thirst."
That which is not sufficient even for filling the belly of one who is weary is considered slightly middling.
The gaze of the Sun, the desired deity of battle, shone with a mass of sparks from his fierce, wide-open, and hard pupils; through its wrath, it took on the form of an ill-omened lightning flash.
O lord of men, it is most wonderful that while your fame whitens the worlds,
it makes your friends devoted and turns the faces of your enemies pale.
Now that my attachment to sense objects has ceased, my mind desires for a long time to be absorbed solely in the Self alone. (ST 3.43d)

The Bhāratīya style consists primarily of the Pradhāna and Puruṣa gaṇas, is filled with excellent crooked sayings (vakrokti), and takes recourse to the heroic, the comic, and the marvelous sentiments.
For the virtuous, birth, death, slaughter, bondage, and so forth are equal to those of others;
yet even so, their fortunes are vast and immovable.
In this case, the sole cause is a total devotion to rashness.
May the secret and profound laughter of Hari, the teacher of those who harm the world, while he was under Yaśodā’s protection in his childhood, purify you.
Although this king is fearless, he bestows his own bright fame upon his enemies in battle; that he takes it from them is truly wonderful.
Having observed such delightful modes of expression,
having seen the compositions of the great poets, and having perceived this variety, one should compose [this work].
Poetry is a thief of the hearts of the virtuous.
Poetry that is tasteless, antagonistic, difficult to reconcile in its sentiment, devoid of aesthetic flavor, or marred by a defective recipient is not praised by the wise.
"O innocent one, casting aside the grief for your mother's death,
clearly honor your youth with me"— such words are considered distasteful.
Where a single rasa is carried through a composition without interruption, some desire that it reach great expansion; yet others consider such a work to be devoid of rasa.
During sexual union, I drink from her face, whose cheeks are drenched with the foul pus oozing from nail-marks; that is called the "counter-attack" (pratyanīka).
Go instead to that very woman who is unaccustomed to you, for she has been set ablaze on your account.
O rogue, what business have you with me? This [affair] of yours is merely a taste for treacherous intrigue.
"The wicked man is indeed beloved; the mind-born god [Kāma] has withered my heart;
I am emaciated by the torment of separation from her"—such words are devoid of flavor. (ST 3.51)
A naive girl [is so] without artifice; a courtesan is skilled in sexual union;
a woman of good family is always bold—it is considered that this [latter case] is a defect of the recipient. (ST 3.52)
These defects should be avoided by the wise even in other aesthetic sentiments (*rasas*),
so that through their contact the poem does not fail to proceed through a succession of *rasas*.
Thus, by this path described by me,
which leads to the entirety of the specific aesthetic flavor (*rasa*),
[the poem] is adorned with charming metrical feet and poetic figures.
In this world, for those of perfected intellect, speech behaves like a woman.
This work, named *Śṛṅgāratilaka*, has been composed by me; let poets and lovers study it for the sake of their proficiency. (ST 3.55)
What other poetic discourse is there, what kind of wit, what arrival of aesthetic flavor,
and alas, what ornament for the literary assembly, without the *Śṛṅgāratilaka*?
Rudra again propitiates Umā— who had attained joy solely from the destruction of Tripura and who is worshipped by all the gods— by means of the ritual of the *Śṛṅgāratilaka*.

Thus ends the third chapter, titled "The Description of the Comic and Other Rasas," in the work called *Śṛṅgāratilaka*, a treatise on the aesthetic flavors and ornaments of poetry composed by the venerable Rudraṭa.
